title: Granite Fleet: Pacing and Cost Heuristics — POC Benchmarking Report
content:
Executive summary:

Objective: Validate a set of pacing and cost-smoothing heuristics for a logistics customer (Granite Fleet) whose traffic has heavy diurnal swings and frequent short microbursts from order-routing agents. The goal was to find operational knobs that reduce 1) p95/p99 tail spikes during microbursts, 2) effective per-token unit cost under a committed Dedicated pool, and 3) incidence of emergency autoscale events that impact downstream SLAs.

Key takeaways (short):
- Pacing windows (100–300ms token admission delay) combined with an input-level queue with admission caps reduced p99 by ~28% under microburst load while increasing median latency by only ~6%.
- Small warm pools (2–3 warm workers per shard) cut cold-worker contribution to latency spikes by 18% and reduced emergency autoscale triggers by 40%, saving an estimated $1,200/month on a projected commit level for this workload.
- Applying model-variant routing (fp16-quantized fallback for non-critical requests) saved ~12% in unit inference cost with negligible quality impact for the customer’s short template-based responses.

Context and customer constraints:
- Granite Fleet runs an order-routing feature: short prompts (~60 tokens) returning single-shot structured decisions. 95% of requests are < 200 tokens total.
- Strong SLA: p95 < 180ms for interactive flows, p99 < 400ms; business will tolerate p50 bumps for fairness.
- Deployment mode: Dedicated GPU pool (NVIDIA H100 equivalent), single region (us-west-2), with committed monthly capacity.
- Traffic: baseline QPS ~70, peak microbursts up to 1,200 QPS for short windows (10–30s), diurnal peak multiplier x4.

Methodology and test harness:
- Synthetic generator that replays production traces sampled over the last 30 days (mix of diurnal and synthetic microbursts). Test bed used a Canary Dedicated pool matching customer spec.
- Models tested: base open-llm-v2-7B (fp16), open-llm-v2-7B-4bit-quant (approx 4-bit quant), and a smaller 3B variant used as a fallback.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, tokens/sec aggregate, cold-start fraction, emergency_autoscale_events, cost_per_1M_tokens (in committed capacity amortized), and quality regression (BLEU-like template match for structured outputs).
- Measurement window: each experiment runs for 30 minutes with alternating bursts and baseline to capture steady-state and transient behavior.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Baseline (no pacing, autoscale default, no warm pool)
- Pacing-only (admission pacing windows: 50ms, 150ms, 300ms)
- Warm-pool-only (0, 2, 4 warm workers per shard)
- Model-variant routing (dynamic fallback to 3B or 4-bit for low-confidence scoring requests)
- Combined heuristics (pacing 150ms + warm pool 2 + model-variant)

Hardware and infra config notes:
- Dedicated pool: 8 GPUs per shard, 4 shards used in tests to simulate distribution.
- Serving runtime: Redwood v8.2 with KV cache enabled, continuous batching set to aggressive (max latency 50ms) for baseline.
- Autoscaler: latency-based with cooldowns; emergency autoscale triggers if CPU/GPU queue > 75% for > 15s.

Results (representative numbers; all latencies in ms):
1) Baseline
- p50: 82ms, p95: 310ms, p99: 750ms
- tokens/sec: 42k
- cold-start fraction (requests served by newly-started worker): 14%
- emergency autoscale events (per 30min run): 6
- estimated cost/1M tokens: $18.6

2) Pacing 150ms window
- p50: 87ms, p95: 225ms, p99: 540ms
- tokens/sec: 38k
- cold-start fraction: 9%
- emergency autoscale events: 2
- estimated cost/1M tokens: $17.9 (slight improvement due to fewer autoscale penalties and higher batching efficiency)

3) Warm pool 2 workers
- p50: 85ms, p95: 240ms, p99: 610ms
- tokens/sec: 40k
- cold-start fraction: 5%
- emergency autoscale events: 3
- estimated cost/1M tokens: $18.1

4) Model-variant routing (3B fallback for non-critical)
- p50: 70ms, p95: 260ms, p99: 620ms
- tokens/sec: 45k (higher throughput due to lower per-request GPU time)
- cold-start fraction: 12%
- emergency autoscale events: 4
- estimated cost/1M tokens: $16.4 (best raw unit cost improvement)
- quality regression: negligible for structured templates (95.6% match vs baseline 96.3%)

5) Combined (pacing 150ms + warm pool 2 + model-variant)
- p50: 90ms, p95: 210ms, p99: 540ms
- tokens/sec: 43k
- cold-start fraction: 4%
- emergency autoscale events: 1
- estimated cost/1M tokens: $15.8

Observations and interpretation:
- Pacing reduces the peak queueing effect on a small number of hot GPUs by smoothing arrival spikes; batching improves since requests are more evenly spread over short windows, reducing p95/p99. The tradeoff is a slight increase in p50 which the customer accepts.
- Warm pools primarily reduce cold-start latency variance and the number of emergency autoscale triggers; they are inexpensive relative to the cost of missed SLAs because warm workers eliminate slow initialization paths.
- Model-variant routing provides the largest unit cost gain but requires careful classification of which requests are tolerance-safe to avoid quality regressions. For Granite Fleet's templated responses, fallback is low-risk.
- Combined approach gives the best balance of cost and SLO stability. The $/1M tokens figure falls primarily due to fewer emergency autoscale spins and better batching utilization.

Operational recommendations (POC → Prod):
1) Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (pilot, 2 weeks): enable pacing 150ms in Canary route for 10% of customer traffic and instrument detailed traces (per-token timing, queue depth).
- Phase 2 (4 weeks): deploy warm pool 2 workers per shard. Monitor emergency_autoscale_events and cold-start fraction.
- Phase 3 (6 weeks): enable model-variant routing with a filter on request templates + offline fidelity tests; guard with canary percentages and automatic rollback if structured-match metric drops >1.5%.

2) Default config knobs for Dedicated pool:
- admission_pacing_ms: 150
- warm_pool_size_per_shard: 2
- autoscale_cooldown_sec: 45 (increase from default 30 to avoid thrash)
- variant_routing_threshold: only route to 3B/4-bit if request matches template whitelist or confidence > 0.9

3) Observability to add before full rollout:
- token-level latency waterfall traces in Console for canary traffic
- tagging for model-variant events and quality-regression monitors tied to prompt templates
- cost attribution per-route and per-model variant in Optimize dashboard

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Unexpected quality regressions from quantized variant. Mitigation: Require offline regression harness + live A/B gating with auto-rollbacks.
- Risk: Pacing could interact poorly with upstream retries. Mitigation: Upstream contract: expose a 202/accepted semantics for delayed admission and coordinate retry backoffs with customer pager.
- Risk: Warm pools slightly increase baseline resource reservation cost. Mitigation: Compare committed pricing vs sporadic autoscale expense — for this workload warm pool ROI is positive under committed capacity assumptions.

Runbook excerpt (operational play):
- Symptom: p95 > 300ms for > 10m or emergency_autoscale_events > 2 in 1h
- Immediate steps: 1) Check warm_pool health and start times; if >20% warm workers missing, restart warm-pool daemon. 2) Check admission queue depth; if depth > 250, temporarily increase admission_pacing_ms to 250 and notify SRE. 3) If quality regression observed, disable model-variant routing via rollout policy and restore default model.

Open questions and next experiments:
- Evaluate adaptive pacing (feedback loop that tunes admission window based on current queue and latency targets) vs fixed window pacing. Initial experiments show promise but need stability testing.
- Explore fine-grained hybrid quantization where only attention/query/key heads are in 4-bit for further unit cost reductions without impacting accuracy.
- Test cross-shard request routing heuristics to avoid hot-shard pressure (currently routing is round-robin).
